astra.text:
Yeah, so I think Tau-bench is very much connected to this question of, like, what happens when you actually put these agents in the real world, right? Customer support sounds like you’re just answering questions, but really you’re trying to help somebody accomplish something. You have to understand what they want, interact with tools, and follow the policies of the business. And all of those things have to work together.

The other piece is that the user is part of the environment. It’s not just, here’s a question, go away and come back with an answer. You might need to ask for information. The user might clarify something, or change what they want halfway through. So the motivation was to capture that interaction between the agent, the user, and the tools, and evaluate whether the agent actually gets the task done. Because you can have a very nice-sounding conversation and still not accomplish what the user needed, right?

And I think reliability is a really interesting part of this. In research, you’re often excited when something works once. That tells you something is possible. But when you’re deploying a system, you need it to work consistently. If you give it the same situation again, does it still make the right decisions? That’s a different bar, and I think benchmarks need to reflect that more.

In terms of what should exist, I’d love to see more tasks where the agent has to work over a longer period of time. Not just a longer conversation, but actually maintain context, make progress, and come back to something after getting new information. And where the goals aren’t completely spelled out at the beginning. Humans don’t always give you this perfectly specified task, right? Part of being useful is figuring out what you need to ask before you act.

But I’d connect that back to what I was saying earlier: I don’t think making a benchmark harder is enough by itself. You want to ask, what’s a useful thing we’d really like these systems to do that we’re not measuring yet? And then build an environment that captures the important difficulties of that. That’s the part I get excited about. These models have so much knowledge already; the question is how well they can use it to accomplish something in an environment that keeps changing.

sol.text:
Yeah, so Tau Bench really came out of seeing the gap between the way we evaluated agents in research and what actually mattered when you deployed one. In a benchmark, we often give an agent a fairly clean task, it produces an answer, and we decide whether that answer looks correct. But a customer-support agent has to interact with a user over multiple turns, understand what they actually want, follow the company’s policies, use tools, and make the right changes in the underlying system. It can’t just sound helpful—it has to complete the task correctly and consistently.

So the motivation was to build something much closer to that reality. Can the agent navigate a conversation, make decisions under constraints, and reliably achieve the right outcome? And reliability is really important here. If an agent succeeds once but fails when you ask the same thing in a slightly different way, that’s not something you can comfortably deploy.

More broadly, I think we still need benchmarks with much longer horizons and much more realistic consequences. Most current tasks have a relatively clear endpoint and are completed in one session. But useful agents may need to work for hours or days, recover from mistakes, ask for clarification, coordinate across different tools, and recognize when they should stop or hand the task to a human. I’d also like benchmarks where the environment changes and where success isn’t captured by one exact answer. Those are harder to build and evaluate, but they’re much closer to what real agents will eventually have to do.

r004.rationale: It clearly presents Tau Bench as a benchmark intended to evaluate AI agents on conversations, tool use, constraints, and task outcomes.

opus.text:
Yeah, so Tau-Bench came out of, like, a very concrete frustration, honestly. So when I got to Sierra, right, you're suddenly looking at, like, actual production traffic. Real customers talking to these agents. And then you go look at the benchmarks that the field has, and there's just, like, a massive mismatch, right? So at that point most of the tool-use benchmarks, they were basically single turn. You give the model a query, it emits a function call, you check if the function call matches some ground truth. And that's, that's just not what's happening, right? Like in reality the user comes in, they say something vague like, "My order is wrong." And the agent has to go back and forth, ask for the email, pull up the order, figure out that actually they wanna exchange, not return, and then there's, like, a 20-page policy document from the company that says you can only do this if the order hasn't shipped, right?

So there were kind of three things we really wanted to capture. One is the multi-turn dynamic interaction with the user, and so we, we simulate the user with an LLM, which is imperfect, but it lets you actually get that back and forth. Second is the policy adherence piece, which I think is really underrated. Like, a lot of the failures we saw were not the model being dumb. The model is smart. It's the model being helpful in a way that violates the rules, right? It just, like, gives the customer a refund because the customer asked nicely. And that's, that's a real business problem. And then third, we evaluate on database state, not on the text. So at the end, did the world actually change the way it was supposed to? Because you can have an agent that says all the right things and does nothing.

And then the thing I'm actually, like, most proud of in that paper is the pass^k metric. So instead of running the task once, you run it k times and you ask, did it succeed every single time? And the numbers just fall off a cliff, right? Like, you go from something respectable at pass^1 to, like, near zero at pass^8 on some of these. And that, that was the real message, I think. Reliability is the bottleneck, not capability. If you're a company deploying this, you don't care that it works 70% of the time. You care that it works the same way every time.

On what's missing, I'd say a few things. The big one for me is long horizon. Like everything we have is, what, tens of steps, maybe a hundred? I want benchmarks where the agent is working on something for days, and it has to maintain context, come back to things, remember what it decided on Tuesday. We have basically nothing there. Related to that is, like, learning over time. Right now every eval episode is amnesiac. The agent starts fresh. But a human employee gets better at their job in month three than month one, and there's no benchmark that measures that at all.

The second thing is tasks where you can't write a verifier. Like, I think we've been somewhat, uh, drawn to the light of, of verifiable domains, right? Math, code, database state. Because it's easy. But a huge fraction of valuable work is, like, "write me a good research report," or "design this," and the quality is genuinely subjective. And I don't think we have a good methodology for that yet. Maybe it's rubrics, maybe it's human preference at scale, I don't know.

And then the last one, honestly, is cost. Like, we report accuracy and we just, we don't report the number of tokens or the latency or the dollars. And in the real world, an agent that's two points better and 10x more expensive is not better. So I'd love to see benchmarks that treat that as a first-class axis rather than a footnote in the appendix.

grok.text:
Yeah, so Tau-Bench, I think, really came out of that same sort of motivation I was talking about earlier, right? Like, you don't want research to just stop at publishing a paper. At Sierra you're actually seeing these agents get deployed in the real world, in the enterprise, customer support, all of that. And suddenly the question is not, like, can the model write a nice paragraph or play an Atari game. It's, can it actually sit in a realistic workflow and be useful.

And that's the same flavor as WebShop, SWE-Bench, right? Those were all trying to push towards, hey, what is useful in a real-world kind of scenario. Not just answering questions. Language doesn't exist in isolation, so you shouldn't evaluate it in isolation. With Tau-Bench it was like, okay, there's a user on the other side, there are tools, there are policies, there's a task that actually looks like something an enterprise agent would have to do. Can these systems handle that? And I think that was the gap we were trying to close. Imagine one or two steps into the future and bring it closer to what we're seeing now.

I wouldn't say I'm specifically oriented towards benchmarking, right? It's a cycle. You put out the right tasks, that tells you what's missing, then you go build the methods, and so on. But you do want new tasks that these systems should be performing, and you want them to have impact, even if it's a few years down the line.

And on the second part, like, what should exist that doesn't yet. Honestly, I think the benchmarks we have are probably a pretty low ceiling for these models. They can do so much more. So I'd love to see things that are more realistic, longer horizon, more grounded. Not a single session, not a toy environment. An agent that has to operate in the world, maybe with other agents, which, you know, going way back, that was actually what I started on at OpenAI, multi-agent coordination and communication.

And also the reliability side. Same thing as the old RL motivation, POLCO and all of that. If you're deploying in a critical setting, you can't have the thing mess up thousands of times. So how do you even measure whether these agents are actually robust when it matters? I think that's still pretty open. Push the envelope, define the area, close the gap. That's the flow, basically.

gemini.text:
Yeah, so Tau-Bench really came out of that direct realization of what’s actually missing when you try to deploy agents in the real world, especially after seeing the kinds of challenges you face at a place like Sierra. 

If you look at the existing benchmarks for tool use or conversational agents at the time, most of them were either very static or essentially single-turn—like, here’s an instruction, call this API, and you're done. Or they assumed a completely cooperative, robotic user who gives you all the information in a neat little package right at the start. 

In reality, real-world interactions are messy. We call it TAU-Bench because it evaluates the interaction between the Tool, the Agent, and the User. First, users are dynamic and ambiguous—they change their minds, they provide partial info, or they ask questions halfway through. Second, the agent has to navigate complex enterprise policies—like, you can only issue a refund if the item was purchased within 30 days and meets specific conditions, otherwise you have to offer store credit. And third, the agent has to execute stateful API calls correctly based on that conversation. When we evaluated frontier models on it, even the best models struggled significantly compared to humans because juggling dynamic user intent, multi-step tool use, and strict policy adherence simultaneously is really hard.

As for benchmarks that don’t exist yet that I think should exist—there are a couple of areas I'm really excited about. 

One is lifelong or continuous learning benchmarks for agents. Almost everything we evaluate today is purely episodic and stateless: the agent gets an environment, tries to solve the task, and then you wipe its memory and reset. But in the real world, an agent should be working over weeks or months. It should make a mistake, receive feedback, adapt its strategy, and remember that constraint the next time it encounters a similar situation. We don't really have good, standardized benchmarks for measuring how well agents learn and adapt continuously without catastrophic forgetting or drifting off policy.

The second area is around truly long-horizon, multi-agent collaboration with human-in-the-loop dynamics. Not just agents talking to other agents in a toy game, but realistic environments where agents have to collaborate with humans, know when to ask for clarification, know when to escalate safely, and operate under high uncertainty. I think moving from these short-horizon, isolated task benchmarks toward continuous, interactive, and evolving environments is really where the evaluation frontier needs to go.

kimi.text:
Yeah, so tau bench came, like, pretty directly out of the Sierra experience, right? Like, once you're actually deploying agents for enterprises, you very quickly realize that the benchmarks the community had, including honestly some of the ones we had made, right, like WebShop, were missing some really key aspects of what a real deployment looks like. So a couple of things come to mind. One is the task is never just like a single clean instruction, right? A user comes in, half the time they don't even know what they want. The conversation is dynamic, so the agent has to sort of roll with that, ask clarifying questions, handle people changing their mind midway, all that. The second is there's a policy, right? Like, enterprises have these very specific rules, like you can refund this but not that, and the agent has to follow them exactly even when the user is pushing really hard in a different direction. And then obviously there's tools and actually mutating real state, a real database, right? So mistakes actually matter.

But I think the biggest thing for me was reliability. Once you deploy, you realize with, like, brutal clarity that it doesn't matter if your agent solves something 60 percent of the time, right? That's a failing product. The same task, run the same agent twice, you get different outcomes. So tau bench was really designed around that, to sort of hammer this consistency angle, like can the agent do it reliably across many independent trials? And the numbers were honestly pretty sobering. Even the best models at the time were succeeding, like, less than half the time, and once you asked for consistency, way lower. And it matched almost exactly what we were seeing in the real world. So for me it was this really nice loop of research informing the product and the product problems informing the research. And yeah, credit to Shunyu and Noah who really drove a lot of that.

As for benchmarks that don't exist yet, I'd say the big hole right now is long-lived agents, right? Most of our benchmarks are still one session, one task, done. But the real value proposition is an agent that works with you over weeks or months, builds up memory, learns your preferences and, like, proactively does useful things without being asked. And we genuinely have no idea how to even evaluate that yet. Relatedly, I think handling ambiguity and change, where the environment shifts under you, goals conflict, there's no clean verifiable answer, and it's about judgment. And honestly, knowing when to say "I can't do this" or escalate to a human. Benchmarks that actually reward appropriate abstention. That stuff basically doesn't exist yet, and I think it's what we need to push these systems toward being genuinely trustworthy, not just, you know, impressive on a leaderboard.

fable.text:
Yeah, so Tau-Bench, I think the motivation was pretty simple actually. So when I got to Sierra, right, and I started looking at what these agents actually have to do in the real world, it was pretty clear that most of the benchmarks that existed, including honestly some of the ones that we had built, like WebShop or even SWE-Bench, right, they have this flavor of, like, here's a task, here's an environment, go do it, right? So it's the agent interacting with an environment. But if you actually look at what happens in customer service or, like, any kind of real deployment, there's a third thing in the picture, which is the human, right? There's a user who is talking to the agent, and the user is not gonna give you the task description in one neat paragraph. They're gonna be vague, they're gonna change their mind halfway through, they're gonna forget to tell you their order number, all of that, right?

And then the second thing is, the agent doesn't operate in a vacuum. It has to follow rules, right? Like, the company has a policy. You can only cancel a flight within 24 hours, or you can only exchange an item if it's the same category, whatever it is. And so the agent has to sort of balance, like, being helpful to the user while also, like, actually following the policy and not just doing whatever the user asks. And nobody was measuring that. So I think that was, that was the gap, right? So Tau-Bench was basically, like, let's simulate a user with an LLM, let's give the agent a set of tools, like APIs into a database, and let's give it a policy document, and then let's see if it can actually get the state of the database to the right end state, right? So it's not, like, judged on how nice the conversation sounds. It's like, did you actually do the right thing at the end?

And I think the thing that I was most, I would say, happy about with that paper was actually this metric, pass at k, or pass hat k, right? Where instead of saying, like, did the model solve it once, you ask, like, can the model solve it eight times in a row, right? Because if you're deploying this thing and it works, like, 60% of the time, that's kind of useless in a business setting, right? You need it to be reliable. And what we saw was, like, these numbers just fall off a cliff, right? The model might get, like, 60% pass at one, and then pass at eight is like 20-something. So that was, like, a very clear signal that these models are capable, but they're not consistent. And I think that consistency thing is, like, still one of the biggest gaps, actually.

In terms of benchmarks that should exist, I think there's a few things. One is, like, I think we're still really bad at measuring long horizon stuff, right? Like, most of the tasks, even, like, the harder ones, are like, you know, tens of steps, maybe a hundred steps. But, like, a real job is, like, weeks and months, right? So, like, what does it mean for an agent to work on something over a long time, keep track of state, come back to it, all of that? We don't really have good ways of measuring that. The second thing I would say is, like, learning, right? Like, right now every benchmark treats the agent as, like, a fixed thing. You evaluate it, it doesn't get better. But if you think about a human employee, right, like, the whole point is they get better at the job over time. So I think benchmarks where the agent actually has to improve from experience, from feedback, from, like, past interactions, I think that's, that's pretty important and nobody's really done it well.

And then the third one, which I'm actually pretty excited about, is, like, the human collaboration piece, right? So Tau-Bench has the user, but it's still kind of, like, the user is the one giving the task. I think a more interesting thing is when the agent and the human are actually, like, working on something together, right? Where the agent has to figure out, like, when should I ask a question, when should I just go ahead, when do I need to check in, right? And I think that's, like, a very hard thing to get right, and we don't even really know how to measure it. So, yeah, I think those are the ones that I'd love to see. And I'll say, like, the same thing I said before, right? I think the models are probably way ahead of where the benchmarks are, so, like, the benchmarks kind of need to catch up.
